newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan says no rupee devaluation planned now.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan says no rupee devaluation planned now.

text.p: Pakistani Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz said on Monday that Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government had no plans to devalue the rupee now.
Aziz, quoted by the official APP news agency, told Senate (upper house of parliament) that instead of devaluing the currency, the government was trying to "maintain it at the present level".
His comments in replies to questions from Senators followed a fall in Pakistani stocks on selling pressure triggered by fears of a new rupee devaluation against the dollar.
The fears were sparked by a statement by Aziz in the National Assembly (lower house) on Thursday that a marginal devaluation of the rupee would be inevitable to stabilise the national economy.

The minister said on Monday the value of the rupee had to be adjusted to improve the competitiveness of exports in the international market whenever the rate of inflation in Pakistan was higher than at the international level.
He said an increase in budget deficit could also create demand for imports and make it necessary to adjust the value of the rupee to curtail imports and protect the country's balance of payments.
Earlier on Monday, the State (central) Bank of Pakistan raised forward cover fee on foreign currency deposits placed with it by commercial banks amid fears of a rupee devaluation.
The fee is charged by the SBP for providing exchange risk cover on deposits brought by banks from abroad.

An SBP official said the forward cover fee for dollar deposits had been raised to 5.0 percent per annum from 4.75 percent fixed on April 21, 1996 and for pound sterling to 4.37 percent from 4.04 percent.
Forward cover fee for deutche mark deposits was raised to 7.20 percent from 6.66 percent and for yen deposits to 9.65 percent from 9.13 percent per annum, he said.
SBP did not say why the fee has been raised but bankers said the move might be related to Aziz's Thursday's statement in which he hinted at the possibility of a marginal devaluation.
The Karachi Stock Exchange's 100-share index tumbled 21.43 points, or 1.35 percent, to close at 1,569.87 on Monday on what dealers described as fears of a devaluation of the rupee against the dollar.
